source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.3, printed pages 9-11: the definition, the factors and the trends of ionization energy (Figure 1.6).

blocks.title: First ionization energy
blocks.text: The energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole of atoms of the element in the gaseous state, to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions, is the first ionization energy (delta H i1).

For sodium, Na(g) gives Na+(g) + e-, delta H i1 = 494 kJ per mol; for calcium, Ca(g) gives Ca+(g) + e-, delta H i1 = 590 kJ per mol. If a second electron is removed from each ion in a mole of gaseous 1+ ions, that is the second ionization energy: Ca+(g) gives Ca2+(g) + e-, delta H i2 = 1150 kJ per mol. Removing a third electron from each 2+ ion is the third ionization energy: Ca2+(g) gives Ca3+(g) + e-, delta H i3 = 4940 kJ per mol. An element can have as many ionization energies as its atomic number.

items: Nuclear charge: the greater the effective nuclear charge, the greater the electrostatic attraction and the harder it is to remove an electron, so ionization energy rises with effective nuclear charge.
Size of the atom or ion: in bigger atoms the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons is weaker, so ionization energy falls as the size increases, and vice versa.

Electronic arrangement: half-filled and completely filled orbitals are more stable, so the ionization energy is higher when the electron must come from a fully filled or half-filled shell. The noble gases have the highest ionization energies of their periods because of their stable ns2 np6 shells. Oxygen has a lower ionization energy than nitrogen: nitrogen is 1s2 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz1 (1403 kJ per mol) and oxygen 1s2 2s2 2px2 2py1 2pz1 (1365 kJ per mol); although nitrogen has one unit less nuclear charge, the extra stability of its half-filled subshell makes its electron harder to remove.
Shielding effect: the greater the shielding, the easier it is to remove the valence electrons. The larger the number of inner electrons, the greater the screening and the lower the ionization energy.

Spin-pair repulsion: when two electrons are spin-paired in the same orbital, their repulsion makes it slightly easier to remove one of them than to remove an unpaired electron. Oxygen has two spin-paired electrons in a 2p orbital, so its ionization energy is relatively lower; nitrogen's three 2p electrons are unpaired, so removing one takes more energy.

blocks.text: Going down a group the nuclear charge increases, but the size of the atom and the number of shielding electrons increase too, so the ionization energy decreases from top to bottom. In group 1 the order is Li greater than Na greater than K greater than Rb greater than Cs; the 6s valence electron of cesium is farther from the nucleus and easier to remove than the 5s electron of rubidium. Across a period from left to right the number of shells stays the same while the effective nuclear charge rises, so it becomes harder to remove an electron; the shielding within the same shell is the same and is not counted, so the ionization energy increases. The trend for periods 1 to 3 shows the noble gases with the highest values, because their complete outer shells make removal extremely difficult, and the alkali metals with the lowest.

blocks.alt: A line graph of first ionization energy against the elements from hydrogen to argon: peaks at helium, neon and argon, troughs at lithium and sodium, and small dips at boron, oxygen, aluminium and sulfur. Notes below explain the trend across a period, down a group, the two dips, and the successive ionization energies of calcium.
blocks.caption: The shape of the first ionization energy trend across periods 1 to 3 (original diagram after Figure 1.6; heights follow the trend, values printed are the textbook's).
blocks.long_description: Ionization energy climbs across each period to a peak at the noble gas and drops to a trough at the next alkali metal. Within a period there are two dips: after beryllium and magnesium, when the next electron enters a higher p subshell, and after nitrogen and phosphorus, when the next electron pairs up and spin-pair repulsion makes it easier to remove, which is why oxygen (1365 kJ per mol) is below nitrogen (1403). Down a group the values fall as atoms grow and shielding increases. Successive ionization energies of one element rise, as calcium's 590, 1150 and 4940 kJ per mol show.
